summary.one_line: India's largest digital personal-loan platform by managed AUM, profitable and scaling fast. But every rupee of the Rs.750 crore fresh issue goes into taking on more unsecured credit risk (DLG guarantees and NBFC capital) just as Stage 3 loans have nearly tripled, so this is one to track through a credit cycle rather than buy blind.
bull_points: Scale leader among Indian digital personal-loan platforms: FY25 managed AUM of Rs.16,715 crore versus Navi Rs.11,695 crore, KreditBee Rs.10,102 crore, Fibe Rs.5,268 crore and Kissht Rs.4,087 crore, as compared in the RHP (S9).
Growth is strong and profitable. Revenue from operations rose from Rs.1,342 crore in FY24 to Rs.3,351 crore in FY26, and Q1 FY27 PAT was Rs.173.8 crore against Rs.67.2 crore a year earlier (S1, S12).

Operating leverage is visible. EBITDA/total income went from about 24% in FY24 to about 40% in Q1 FY27, and the RHP says annualised loan losses of 6.95% in FY26 were below the 8.29% industry average (S1, S9).

The user base should keep getting cheaper to monetise: 140.28 million registered users, of whom 11.90 million (8.5%) have taken at least one product, up from 4.62 million monetised users in FY24 (S1).

The litigation record is clean. There are no criminal, tax or regulatory cases against the company or the promoters, and the only matter at a subsidiary is a Rs.19.74 million case the subsidiary itself filed (S1).
bear_points: All Rs.575 crore of identified fresh-issue objects increase credit exposure: Rs.325 crore to back more DLG-guaranteed loans and Rs.250 crore of equity for the lending NBFC. None of it goes to technology or distribution (S1).
Asset quality is getting worse. Gross Stage 3 loans went from 0.94% (Mar-24) to 1.88% (Mar-25), 2.74% (Mar-26) and 2.72% (Jun-26), and the book is entirely unsecured personal loans (S1, S3).

Operating cash flow was negative in every full year: a combined roughly Rs.4,004 crore outflow over FY24-FY26 against about Rs.654 crore of cumulative PAT. Borrowings went from Rs.1,709 crore to Rs.5,485 crore (Jun-26) (S1).

Governance flags before listing. There was a Rs.160 crore one-time incentive to the CEO in FY26 and a Rs.48.32 crore API-breach fraud at subsidiary WFPL, of which only about Rs.2.3 crore has been recovered, and the auditor has flagged audit-trail and back-up lapses (S1, S10, S12).
Promoter skin in the game is thin. The promoter group holds 23.96% before the issue and 20.33% after it, and both founders are selling shares in the OFS (S1, S15).
watch_points: Gross Stage 3 and impairment cost trend in the first two listed quarters. The FY26 impairment ratio was 5.16% of average managed AUM (S18).
Outstanding DLG: Rs.1,060.78 crore, or 43.92% of net worth, in June 2026. Watch it both in absolute terms and against net worth as the Rs.325 crore DLG object is spent (S18).
Any RBI change to digital-lending, DLG or unsecured-credit risk-weight rules. DLG is capped at 5% of the covered portfolio under the June 2023 circular (S20, S27).
Anchor lock-in expiries at 30 and 90 days after allotment, and the concentration of VC holders who remain after the OFS (S11, S26).

reasoning: The fresh money buys more credit risk, not more moat. Rs.325 crore expands DLG-guaranteed disbursals, where Moneyview absorbs first losses of up to 5% of partner portfolios, and Rs.250 crore capitalises the NBFC that holds unsecured loans on its own books. An investor applying is funding balance-sheet risk-taking, so conviction depends on believing the underwriting will hold through a downturn. That has not been tested at this scale (S1, S20).

Credit quality is moving the wrong way even in a benign period. Gross Stage 3 roughly tripled from 0.94% to 2.72% in about two years. Outstanding DLG is already 43.92% of net worth. The better-than-industry loss rate (6.95% vs 8.29% in FY26) is a positive, but it is a relative number from a single cycle (S1, S9, S18).

The business itself is real and good. It is the AUM leader among Indian digital lenders, revenue grew roughly 2.5x in two years, and Q1 FY27 profit was Rs.173.8 crore. The moat is scale, data and a low-cost user funnel, not a regulatory or technical barrier. The 48 financial partners can switch volume, and fee rates are renegotiated periodically (S1, S3, S9, S12).

Governance is acceptable but not clean. The Rs.160 crore CEO incentive paid just before the IPO consumed a large share of FY26 profit. The Rs.48 crore cyber fraud at the lending subsidiary and repeated auditor remarks on audit trails point to control gaps in a company that moves money for millions of borrowers. Promoters will own only about 20% after listing (S1, S10, S12, S15).

What would turn this into an invest call: two or three listed quarters with Stage 3 stable or falling as the DLG book grows, operating cash flow nearing break-even as fee income recovers its share, and no further control incidents. Until then, track (S1).

subsections.title: What Moneyview does and who it serves

blocks.text: Moneyview describes itself as a consumer-focused, digital-only, credit-led financial services platform for 'Middle India', meaning households earning Rs.300,000 to Rs.1,100,000 a year. Its Moneyview mobile app gives access to financial products supplied by a network of banks, NBFCs (including its own NBFC subsidiary), insurers and others that it calls Financial Partners. As of June 30, 2026 it had 140.28 million registered users and 48 Financial Partners (S1). It was founded in 2014 as Whizdm Innovations Pvt Ltd, renamed in May 2025 and converted to a public company in June 2025 (S3).

Personal loans are the flagship product. Moneyview acts as a lending service provider (LSP): it runs user acquisition, evaluation, onboarding, collections and servicing, and a regulated lender funds the loan. Loans are instant and fully digital, up to Rs.1 million with tenures up to 60 months. They are underwritten with in-house AI/ML models that the DRHP says assess over 100,000 variables per user (S1, S3). Since August 2024 the platform has added earned wage access, home loans, credit cards, insurance, digital gold, a fixed-deposit marketplace, UPI and bill payments (S1, S3). Personal loans remain the economic engine.

The typical monetised customer is young and outside the metros. At June 30, 2026, monetised users had an average monthly income of Rs.46,517.55 and an average age of 32, and 79.54% lived in Tier 2 and smaller cities. The company has no branches and served users in 99.04% of India's pin codes (S1). Moneyview says it processes close to 200,000 loan applications a day (S3).

blocks.caption: Platform scale (RHP KPIs, certified by Bashetty & Joshi)

blocks.text: 'Monetised users' is cumulative since inception: anyone who has ever taken a revenue-generating product. It is not the count of currently active borrowers. At 11.90 million out of 140.28 million, about 8.5% of registered users have ever been monetised (S1).

subsections.title: How the money is earned: fees versus interest

blocks.text: Moneyview earns revenue in two ways. (1) Fee and commission income, paid by partner banks and NBFCs for loans originated and serviced through the platform (off-balance-sheet for Moneyview). (2) Interest income on loans held on the books of its wholly owned NBFC subsidiary, Whizdm Finance Pvt Ltd (WFPL), which began on-balance-sheet lending in FY20 (S1, S3). In the RHP the company reports one segment under Ind AS 108 (S1).

blocks.caption: Fees and commission as % of revenue from operations

blocks.text: The mix shows the key strategic shift. In FY23, interest income was only 6.91% of revenue and fees were 91.84% (S3). By FY26, fees had fallen to 56.68% (S1). The company went from an almost pure marketplace to a hybrid that carries credit risk directly through WFPL's book and indirectly through default loss guarantees (DLG) to partners. In Q1 FY27, fee and commission income was Rs.632.9 crore, up 61.5% year on year, and interest income was Rs.387.2 crore, up 36.9% (S12). Fees regained some share that quarter, which the company will point to.

Management frames the current business as about 75% partner-led (loans on partners' books) and 25% originated by its own NBFC (S7). Even the 'partner-led' portion is not risk-free. Under DLG arrangements, Moneyview compensates partners for first losses of up to 5% of the covered portfolio. RBI rules require the guarantee to be backed by cash, a lien-marked FD or a bank guarantee, and it is invoked within 120 days overdue (S20). DLG expense rose from nil in FY23 to about 15-16% of total expenses by FY25-9M FY26 (S3).

The 'capital-light marketplace' label in the offer document's strengths list (S1) is less true every year. Between WFPL's own unsecured book and outstanding DLG of Rs.1,060.78 crore (43.92% of net worth, June 2026), Moneyview now carries a meaningful share of the credit risk on the loans it originates (S18).

subsections.title: Partners, concentration and the operating model

blocks.text: The supply side is its lending partners. The DRHP (March 2026) cited 22 regulated-entity lending partners including its own NBFC (S5) and 42 Financial Partners in total (S3). The RHP counts 48 Financial Partners (S1). Moneyview supplies the customer, the underwriting model and servicing. Partners supply capital and the regulated balance sheet, and pay a fee per loan. The DRHP notes that fee rates carry no long-term contractual guarantee and are 'periodically renegotiated' (S3).

blocks.caption: Revenue concentration by Financial Partner (% of revenue from operations)

blocks.text: Concentration has fallen materially, from 56.78% for the top ten in FY24 to 37.36% in FY26. Some of that is because interest income from WFPL's own book grew (S1). Losing one large bank partner would still hurt, but no single relationship now looks existential. The company has one office, a registered and corporate office in Marathahalli, Bengaluru, and no other physical footprint (S1). Operations are software and people: collections, servicing and onboarding all run digitally.

items: Funding for WFPL comes from wholesale borrowing. Consolidated borrowings rose from Rs.1,709 crore (FY24) to Rs.5,485 crore (June 2026) (S1).

Stated strategies are to grow the registered user base, raise monetisation and personal-loan volumes, cross-sell other products, deepen the partner ecosystem and invest in AI for operating efficiency (S1).
RBI requires WFPL to maintain a minimum CRAR of 15% (S18). The Rs.250 crore capital infusion from the IPO is aimed at this constraint (S1).

blocks.text: The RHP's industry chapter is based on a Redseer report commissioned for the IPO. It projects India's retail loan sanctions to grow at a 13-15% CAGR, from Rs.76.6 trillion in FY2026 to Rs.138-151 trillion by FY2031P. Unsecured loans are projected to grow at 17-19% a year and personal loans to reach Rs.33-36 trillion (S1). Digital personal loans were about 15% of unsecured personal loans sanctioned in FY2026 and are the fastest-growing segment, projected at a 26-27% CAGR over FY2026-FY2031P (S1, S7).

These are commissioned forecasts paid for as part of the offer process. They are directionally plausible given the low credit penetration in Middle India, but they assume a smooth credit cycle. Unsecured retail lending in India has been through regulator-driven slowdowns before. An India Ratings release notes WFPL's capital adequacy fell to 22.7% by end-Q1 FY25 after RBI's November 16, 2023 circular raising risk weights on consumer credit (S27).

Moneyview's growth has broadly tracked or beaten these forecasts. Disbursals grew 31% in FY26 to Rs.23,099 crore and 40% in Q1 FY27 to Rs.7,152 crore (S1, S7). The addressable market is not the constraint. Capital, partner appetite and credit quality are.

The direct competitors are other app-based personal-loan platforms, mostly unlisted: Navi (lends from its own NBFC), KreditBee (small-ticket loans for young salaried borrowers), Fibe (formerly EarlySalary) and Kissht (S9). Moneyview also competes indirectly with bank and NBFC in-house digital lending (e.g. Bajaj Finance) and with fintech distributors such as PB Fintech and Paytm, which the RHP uses as listed peers (S3, S9).

blocks.caption: FY25 managed AUM, digital-lending peer set (as compared in RHP)

blocks.text: On the RHP's numbers, Moneyview is clearly the largest pure digital personal-loan platform by AUM. It is about 43% larger than Navi and more than three times Fibe and Kissht (S9). Its total income grew at a 56.5% CAGR over FY24-FY26, faster than every listed peer the RHP shows (S9). The comparison is company-selected: rival data comes from the same commissioned report, and several peers are private with limited disclosure.

There is no regulatory or technical moat in the strict sense. Any NBFC-backed app can register as an LSP under RBI's digital-lending framework, and the partner banks can and do work with several platforms at once. There is no import-substitution or licence-scarcity angle.

What Moneyview does have is a scale and data advantage. First, 140 million registered users, many acquired through its money-management features, so later loans cost less to acquire than for a pure lending app (S1, S9). Second, underwriting data from about a decade of lending. The RHP says FY26 annualised loss rates were 6.95% against an 8.29% industry average, and 7.07% against 9.35% in FY25 (S9). If that loss gap persists, it is the closest thing to a moat. Partners route volume to the platform that loses them the least money.

Verdict on moat: modest, execution-based and not structural. Scale and underwriting data give an edge that can be copied over time. The edge is only proven for FY24-FY26, a relatively benign period for credit, and Moneyview's own Stage 3 ratio nearly tripled over the same period (S1, S9).

blocks.caption: Restated consolidated summary (Rs. million) from RHP dated Sep 20, 2026
rows: Profit before exceptional items (net of tax)

blocks.text: Revenue from operations grew 74% in FY25 and 43% in FY26, roughly 2.5x in two years (S1). Reported PAT was almost flat in FY26 (Rs.242.7 crore vs Rs.240.3 crore) only because of Rs.206.65 crore of exceptional losses. These were a Rs.160 crore one-time performance incentive to MD & CEO Puneet Agarwal and a Rs.46.65 crore loss from a cyber incident at WFPL (S1, S12). Excluding them, FY26 PAT was Rs.397.3 crore, up about 65% (S1, S12). Q1 FY27 continued the trend: PAT of Rs.173.8 crore against Rs.67.2 crore, and EBITDA up 88% (S12). RoNW figures for the quarters (*) are not annualised. Annualised Q1 FY27 ROE was about 29.9% (S18).

Some of the operating leverage is real. The DRHP showed operating expenses falling from 62.84% of income in FY23 to 35.19% in 9M FY26, while loan margins rose from 7.66% to 8.45% (S3). Q1 FY27 margins were also helped by fees regaining share and by impairment costs growing (30%) more slowly than revenue (50%). Impairment of financial instruments, which includes write-offs and DLG losses, was Rs.261.4 crore in the quarter (S12). A single strong quarter should not be extrapolated.

subsections.title: Balance sheet, leverage and asset quality

blocks.caption: Balance sheet and credit indicators
rows: Gross Stage 3 loans (% of gross loans)

blocks.text: Leverage has risen quickly as WFPL's book grew. Borrowings tripled from FY24 to FY26, and debt/equity was about 2.3x in June 2026 (S1, S18). That is modest for a lending NBFC but a big change from an asset-light marketplace. Gross Stage 3 roughly tripled between March 2024 and March 2026 and has stayed at 2.72%. Net Stage 3 was 0.59% at June 2026 (S1, S12). The DRHP showed provision coverage slipping from 80.49% (FY24) to 75.50% (FY25 and 9M FY26) (S3). The FY26 impairment ratio was 5.16% of average managed AUM (S18).

Off-balance-sheet risk has to be added on top. Outstanding DLG was Rs.1,060.78 crore in June 2026, 43.92% of consolidated net worth (S18), up from Rs.456.3 crore at FY24 and Rs.847.1 crore at December 2025 (S3). DLG is capped at 5% of each covered portfolio (S20). A sharp rise in partner-book defaults would therefore hit Moneyview's P&L even on loans it does not hold.

Asset quality is the key financial variable here. Stage 3 at 2.7% on an all-unsecured book is not alarming in isolation. The direction is the concern, and it comes from a book that is mostly less than two years old.

Over FY24-FY26 the group reported about Rs.654 crore of cumulative PAT but about Rs.4,004 crore of cumulative operating cash outflow, funded by about Rs.4,825 crore of financing inflows, mostly borrowing (S1). For a lender, loan growth shows up as operating cash outflow, so a negative CFO is expected and is not an accounting red flag in itself. The RHP lists negative operating cash flow as a top-ten risk (S1). The practical point is that the growth story depends on continued access to wholesale debt and on regular equity top-ups, which is exactly what the IPO provides.

Q1 FY27 was the first period in the disclosure window with positive operating cash flow (Rs.117 crore) (S1). That coincided with a higher fee share of revenue and slower growth in the on-book loan portfolio. Whether it lasts depends on how much the NBFC grows once the Rs.250 crore infusion arrives.
The trend supports the growth story on revenue and pre-exceptional profit. It supports it less on cash generation and asset quality, which is where the risk now sits.

blocks.text: Sources for the table: S1, S2, S6, S8, S13, S15, S23. About 69% of the issue at the upper band is fresh money that goes to the company. The remaining Rs.341.7 crore is secondary sale by existing holders and raises nothing for Moneyview (S1, S8). The issue was cut sharply after the DRHP. The March 2026 draft sought a Rs.1,500 crore fresh issue and an OFS of 13.61 crore shares (S5, S19). The CEO told PTI that strong profit growth and internal cash generation led to the smaller raise (S22).

blocks.caption: Use of net proceeds (Rs. million), RHP
rows: Investment to drive growth in loan disbursals under DLG arrangements
Investment in WFPL (material subsidiary) to augment capital base
[to be finalised; capped at 25% of gross proceeds]

blocks.text: Of the identified objects, Rs.325 crore will fund the cash or deposits that back first-loss guarantees to partner lenders, so partners will lend more against Moneyview's DLG. Rs.250 crore goes as equity into WFPL so it can grow its own unsecured book within the 15% CRAR requirement (S1, S18). In the DRHP these objects were Rs.650 crore and Rs.450 crore (S5). Both were roughly halved along with the issue. After issue expenses, the balance goes to general corporate purposes. The CEO has said about 75% of the fresh issue will grow lending and the rest will go to new products, technology, AI and IT infrastructure (S22).

Both objects are 'working capital for credit risk', and neither has been appraised by a bank or financial institution (S3). The DLG object is especially notable. IPO money will sit as collateral behind loans on other lenders' books, and it is lost if those loans default. That fits a lending business, but it means retail investors are directly funding first-loss credit exposure.

subsections.title: Who is selling in the OFS

blocks.text: Each founder sells 13.55 million shares, about Rs.46 crore each at the upper band. That is roughly 10% of Puneet Agarwal's and 8.5% of Sanjay Aggarwal's pre-issue holdings (S1). Early VCs are exiting at many times cost. Crimson Winter is the exception: its average cost of Rs.37.42 is above the Rs.34 cap, so it is selling at a loss (S1). The OFS is modest relative to holdings, so this looks like partial profit-taking rather than a rush for the exit. Most VC stakes remain and will become tradeable after listing.

The promoters are Puneet Agarwal (52, MD & CEO, over 23 years in management, operations and fintech), Sanjay Aggarwal (55, Executive Director & CTO, over 19 years in fintech and IT) and Sushma Abburi (53, Chief Product Officer) (S1). Secondary profiles say both co-founders are IIT-Delhi graduates. Puneet Agarwal previously worked at McKinsey, Capital One and Google (as a product management director). Sanjay Aggarwal worked at Infosys and Yahoo and earlier co-founded the ed-tech venture Minglebox (S25). Both founders have run the company since 2014, so tenure and domain relevance are genuine.

Pre-issue, the promoters hold 19.55% (8.66% + 10.33% + 0.56%). The wider promoter group, including the Agarwal Family Trust at 3.05%, takes the total to 23.96% (S1). Chittorgarh puts the post-issue promoter and group holding at 20.33% (S15). The largest holders are VCs: Accel entities at about 21.9% combined, Internet Fund III (Tiger Global) at 13.79%, Ribbit at 10.20% and Apis Growth at 6.61% (S1). This is effectively a professionally run, VC-controlled company with founder management, not a classic promoter-owned business.

subsections.title: Related-party dealings and the CEO incentive

blocks.text: I could not open the full RHP related-party transactions note (see method). From the abridged prospectus and secondary coverage of the RHP, the material related-party items are these. (1) Intra-group funding of the wholly owned NBFC WFPL, which the IPO will increase by Rs.250 crore. This is an eliminated intra-group flow, not a leakage risk (S1). (2) Remuneration to the executive promoters. The standout is a Rs.160 crore one-time performance-based incentive to Puneet Agarwal, charged as an exceptional item in FY26 (S1, S12, S21). (3) A board nominee from the largest investor, Accel. No promoter-owned supplier, customer, lessor or lending entity is disclosed in the sources I could read.

The Rs.160 crore CEO payout is the main governance question. It equals about 40% of FY26 pre-exceptional PAT (Rs.397 crore) and was paid in the fiscal year just before listing. The company describes it as a reward for leadership and contribution to growth (S21). It is disclosed and one-off, so it is not concealment. But it transferred a large amount of shareholder value to a founder who also sells in the OFS, and it sets a precedent that minority holders cannot vote on after the fact (S1, S12).

The weighted average cost of shares bought over the last three years is Rs.0.87, with a range of nil to Rs.64.15. The Rs.64.15 high was an Accel private placement in September 2024 (S1, S3). The Rs.32-34 band is therefore roughly half the price of that September 2024 placement, though Accel's blended cost across all rounds is far lower (Rs.5.32 and Rs.7.65 per share for its two entities). Within the last year, promoter Sushma Abburi acquired shares at a WACA of Rs.0.50 (S1). This is typical of founder ESOP or gift structures, not a red flag on its own.

Outstanding litigation is minimal. There are no criminal, tax, regulatory or material civil proceedings against the company or the promoters, and no SEBI or exchange action against the promoters in five years. Directors face one tax proceeding and one regulatory action. The only subsidiary matter is a criminal complaint WFPL itself filed, involving Rs.19.74 million (S1). The DRHP put the director-level tax matters at Rs.35.73 million (S3).

Internal controls are the weaker area. In August 5-7, 2025, unknown attackers exploited a bank-integrated API at WFPL and bypassed the authorised disbursement mechanism, withdrawing Rs.48.32 crore. Only about Rs.2.35 crore had been recovered by June 30, 2026, and the FY26 exceptional loss was Rs.46.65 crore pre-tax. An FIR was filed and the RBI and CERT-In were notified. A forensic review found no employee involvement (S10). The statutory auditor's CARO annexure for FY26 records this fraud. Its report also notes a missing audit trail at the database layer of one accounting package in FY26, and incomplete daily India-based back-ups and missing audit trails in some software in FY24 and FY25 (S1).

No RBI penalty against WFPL turned up in my searches. However, a Rs.48 crore external breach of a lender's disbursement API, plus audit-trail remarks in three consecutive years, is a genuine control weakness in a business whose core job is moving money safely. These are not boilerplate.

items: Credit-cycle risk on an all-unsecured book. Gross Stage 3 went from 0.94% to 2.72% in about two years, and all WFPL loans are unsecured. A turn in the cycle for young Tier-2 borrowers earning about Rs.46,500 a month would hit both the on-book loans and DLG payouts (S1, S3).

DLG amplification. Outstanding DLG of Rs.1,060.78 crore (43.92% of net worth) will grow as Rs.325 crore of IPO money is deployed. The loss cap is 5% of the covered portfolio, but that cap applies to a much larger partner book than Moneyview's own balance sheet (S18, S20, S1).
Funding dependence. Operating cash flow was negative in FY24-FY26 and borrowings reached Rs.5,485 crore. Growth needs continued wholesale funding at reasonable cost (S1, S3).

blocks.text: These three risks compound each other. In a downturn, credit losses rise, funding tightens and partners pull back at the same time. That is the scenario to test the investment against, and FY24-FY26 does not include it.

items: Regulatory dependence. The model depends on RBI's digital-lending and DLG rules, which have been rewritten several times (2022 guidelines, the 2023 DLG circular, 2025 consolidated directions). RBI has also acted against unsecured consumer credit through risk weights before (S3, S20, S27).

Partner economics. The top ten partners still provide 37-39% of revenue, and fee rates are periodically renegotiated with no long-term guarantee. Partners can reprice or move volume to competitors (S1, S3).
Operational and cyber risk. The Rs.48.32 crore API breach and three years of auditor remarks on audit trails and back-ups show real control gaps (S1, S10).

Key-person and incentive risk. The RHP itself links success to the founders and discloses the Rs.160 crore CEO incentive. Promoters will own about 20% after listing, so VC decisions will largely shape the share register (S1, S15).

blocks.text: Risks deliberately left out as boilerplate: generic 'brand', 'first issue has no market' and 'forward-looking statements' risks. Litigation is also not a material risk here (S1).

In a PTI interview around the price-band announcement, MD & CEO Puneet Agarwal said the issue was cut from Rs.1,500 crore to about Rs.1,092 crore because of strong profit growth and adequate internal cash generation. He cited about Rs.400 crore of FY26 PAT before exceptional items (S22). He said the unsecured-lending opportunity remains significant 'provided growth is backed by disciplined underwriting and risk management'. He also said about 75% of the fresh issue will grow the lending business and the rest will go to new products, technology, AI and IT infrastructure (S7, S22).

The RHP's stated strategies are qualitative, not numerical targets: expand registered users, raise monetisation and personal-loan volumes, deepen multi-product relationships, broaden the partner network, invest in AI for efficiency, and 'drive income growth and cost efficiency to further enhance profitability and return on equity' (S1). The deployment schedule in the objects table is the only hard forward commitment: Rs.375 crore of DLG and NBFC capital in FY27 and Rs.200 crore in FY28 (S1).

Management has given no numeric guidance on disbursals, AUM, credit costs or margins in the sources reviewed. The growth outlook rests on Redseer's 26-27% digital personal-loan CAGR forecast and on recent momentum (Q1 FY27 disbursals +40%, PAT 2.6x), not on company guidance (S1, S12).

subsections.title: Analyst read of the near term

blocks.text: Q1 FY27 gives near-term momentum. Revenue rose 50% and PAT was Rs.173.8 crore, already over 70% of FY26's reported full-year profit, with Stage 3 flat at 2.72% (S12). With fresh DLG and NBFC capital arriving in FY27, disbursal growth should stay high. The variables to watch are whether the fee share of revenue holds near 60% and whether Stage 3 and impairment costs stay contained as the partner-guaranteed book grows (S1, S12).

items: Positive signals would be stable or falling Stage 3, DLG/net worth staying below about 45%, and continued positive operating cash flow (S1, S18).
Negative signals would be Stage 3 rising above 3%, a partner exit or fee cut, any RBI tightening on DLG or unsecured credit, or another control incident (S1, S10, S20).

subsections.title: Anchor book, day-1 status and grey market

blocks.text: On September 23 Moneyview raised Rs.327.5 crore from 12 anchor investors, allotting 9.63 crore shares at Rs.34, the top of the band (S11, S14). Seven domestic mutual funds, through 14 schemes, took 6.96 crore shares, or 72% of the anchor book. SBI Banking & Financial Services Fund took the largest allocation at 1.47 crore shares (about 15.3%, over Rs.50 crore), and HDFC MF also took 1.47 crore shares across three entities (S11). Other anchors included ICICI Prudential, Motilal Oswal, 360 One, Goldman Sachs and Amundi (S11, S14). Anchor shares are locked in under the usual structure: half for 30 days and half for 90 days (S26).

Subscription: this report was written on the opening day, September 24, 2026. The trackers I checked showed the book at 0x overall, 0x retail and 0x NII as of the day-1 snapshot. That means no meaningful data had been posted yet, not that there was no demand. QIB and large-HNI bids usually arrive on the last day (S24). No category-wise figures can be reported yet. The book closes September 28.

GMP is an unofficial grey-market quote with no regulatory standing. It moved from Rs.0-5 to Rs.11 within two days, and it says nothing about credit quality or governance. It is shown for completeness and plays no part in the verdict. A strong anchor book from mainstream mutual funds shows institutional interest, but it does not validate the credit risk being funded.

method: Primary source: the SEBI-hosted Abridged Prospectus (S1), which summarises the RHP dated September 20, 2026. I read every page of it directly. It is the basis for the restated FY24-FY26 and Q1 FY26/FY27 financials, KPIs, the objects table, selling-shareholder and WACA data, shareholding, the board, the top-ten risk factors, auditor remarks and the litigation summary. The full RHP and DRHP PDFs (S4, and the RHP copy on chittorgarh.net) exceed the 10 MB fetch limit and could not be downloaded in this environment. Details normally read in the full document were therefore taken from secondary coverage and cross-checked across at least two outlets where possible: DLG outstanding and history, Stage 3 history and provision coverage, revenue-mix history, peer AUM tables, the cyber-incident breakdown, and the CEO-incentive composition (S3, S9, S10, S12, S18, S21). The detailed related-party transactions note of the RHP could NOT be read. The governance section covers only related-party items visible in the abridged prospectus and news coverage, and does not claim the RPT schedule is otherwise clean. Where secondary sources disagree, I used the abridged prospectus. Two examples: some outlets give PAT in crore to two decimals that differ slightly, and FY26 total assets appear as Rs.8,104.85 crore versus Rs.8,004.85 crore; I omitted total assets. The DRHP-era fees share for FY23 (91.84%) and FY23 DLG/opex data come from a DRHP analysis (S3). Subscription figures reflect a day-1 snapshot showing 0x, meaning no posted data yet. GMP is from unofficial trackers and is not used in the verdict. Valuation metrics (P/E, P/B, market-cap multiples) appeared in several sources and were deliberately excluded. A Business Standard article on the trimmed IPO and some inkl pages returned 403. The Business Standard piece is not cited because it was mainly about valuation. For those, and for S21, S22, S24, S25 and S26, content was taken from search-result snippets rather than a full page read. Where a page carried no clear publication date, the date shown is the access date (2026-09-24). Margin, leverage and cumulative cash-flow ratios labelled as derived are my own arithmetic on S1 figures.
